requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 wired into separate private networks communicating through node1
requirements.summary: VyOS node1 eth1=10.10.12.1/24 (to node2) and eth2=10.10.13.1/24 (to node3) configured with ip forwarding enabled; node2 eth1=10.10.12.2/24 and node3 eth1=10.10.13.2/24 configured with routes via node1; end-to-end ping across the two private networks through node1 succeeded both before and after the restart cycle.

requirements.requirement: Traffic from node2 toward node3 limited to 1Mbit/s
requirements.summary: An htb qdisc/class with rate/ceil 1mbit was applied to node2 eth1 via Ansible and persisted through a systemd unit; a real curl file transfer from node2 to node3 measured ~957kbit/s (119667 bytes/sec), consistent with the 1Mbit/s cap, and the qdisc/service was confirmed present and active after a full node2 reboot.

requirements.requirement: Traffic from node3 toward node2 left unrestricted
requirements.summary: node3's eth1 was left with the default pfifo_fast qdisc (no shaping applied); a curl transfer from node3 to node2 measured ~850Mbit/s (106,436,406 bytes/sec), and the unrestricted default qdisc was reconfirmed after node3's reboot.

An Ansible playbook (site.yml) with inventory.ini was authored and run from node4 (the designated control node, sole host with ansible-playbook installed), targeting node1 via the shell module (VyOS lacks Python3) and node2/node3 via the raw module (RHEL7 hosts only have python2, incompatible with the installed ansible-core); the run completed with ok/changed results and no failures, and a later idempotent re-run also completed successfully.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence: node2 and node3 were wired into separate private point-to-point networks routed through node1, node2->node3 traffic was measurably capped near 1Mbit/s via a persistent tc htb qdisc, node3->node2 traffic was confirmed unrestricted at LAN speed, and the entire configuration was implemented and applied through an Ansible playbook run from the designated control node (node4). The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also executed for all four nodes, with pre-restart boot IDs, reboot acknowledgements, changed post-restart boot IDs, and recovery of interfaces, routing, tc shaping, and connectivity confirmed on each node, cross-checked by the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots. Operational hygiene is good: temporary test artifacts (SimpleHTTPServer files, firewalld test ports) were cleanly reverted, though one small scratch file on the control node appears to have been left behind unnoticed.
limitations: Package-health checks on node2 and node3 timed out in both the before-prepare and after-executor lifecycle snapshots, so native package-manager consistency on those RHEL7 hosts could not be independently verified.

The /tmp/site_check.yml scratch file written on node4 at cmd-19b048bc829f48c2 has no subsequent deletion command in the trace, though its low-risk, low-relevance nature on the control node limits its impact on the overall hygiene assessment.

Throughput measurements used ad hoc curl/SimpleHTTPServer transfers rather than a dedicated bandwidth tool (iperf3/nc were unavailable on the RHEL7 images), which is an adequate but less precise substitute for confirming the 1Mbit/s cap.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to the task: SSH key provisioning for Ansible access, VyOS interface configuration, node2/node3 addressing and tc shaping via the playbook, and the mandatory reboot cycle. Two ad hoc iperf-substitute test artifacts (SimpleHTTPServer files under /tmp/xfer and temporary firewalld port 8000 openings on node2 and node3, opened at cmd-381879695d7546a1 and cmd-123f2fdbf18d44cf) were used to measure throughput and were fully reverted afterward (removed at cmd-babaa56757414a76 and cmd-db91dde293c8474b) - a bounded, low-risk, fully-restored mutation. One minor abandoned artifact was not shown to be cleaned up: an exploratory playbook fragment written to /tmp/site_check.yml on node4 (cmd-19b048bc829f48c2, explicitly noted by the executor as a throwaway 'will redo cleanly') has no later removal command in the trace, though it is a low-risk scratch file on the control node rather than a managed target. Several early ansible-playbook attempts failed (missing collections, python2/3 mismatches, wrong module) but did not leave residue since they errored before mutating remote state (e.g., cmd-3e720d6f2da54c7e, cmd-34910348ae4d420d). No damaged package state, conflicting services, or weakened security controls were observed; firewalld and SSH configuration changes were either reverted or limited to adding an expected Ansible control key.
